title.en: Kahausibware, the Serpent Maker of Bauro
title.zh: 包羅山蛇神卡豪西布瓦勒

region.en: Bauro mountain, San Cristoval, Solomon Islands (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 所羅門群島聖克里斯托瓦爾包羅山（象徵定位）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded by R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians, 1891, ch. X

source.work: R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians: Studies in their Anthropology and Folk-lore (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1891), ch. X 'Spirits'

summary.en: In the infancy of the race, the snake-woman Kahausibware made men, pigs, and every food of San Cristoval, and death had not yet appeared — until she strangled a screaming infant in its mother's absence. Chopped to pieces by the mother's axe, the serpent's parts rejoined again and again until, weeping, she asked who would help them now, and departed across the islands to rest at Marau, leaving the world to deteriorate.
summary.zh: 人類幼年，蛇身婦神卡豪西布瓦勒造人、造豬、造百般食物，聖克里斯托瓦爾島上尚無死亡。一日母親外出，蛇神不耐嬰兒啼哭，以身纏之而窒息。母親歸來，掄斧剁蛇；剁而復合，屢剁屢合，蛇神哭曰：『我走了，誰還幫你們？』遂渡海而去——經烏吉、烏拉瓦至馬勞住下；自此世界事事退化。包羅山之蛇，即其子孫，受人敬奉。

sensitivity.note: Missionary-anthropologist record (Codrington 1891); Arosi heritage of Makira. Snake veneration noted as living custom.

passages.text: Kahausibware was a Hi'ona, a being of superhuman character, dwelling on the mountain of Bauro, the central mass of San Cristoval, in the time of the infancy of the human race. She was a snake in outward form. In those days all the fruits of the earth grew without labour, and all was of the best; it was Kahausibware who made men, pigs, and other animals, cocoa-nuts, fruit-trees, and all the food with which the island is now furnished, and death had not yet appeared.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. X (1891); not verbatim.

passages.text: The woman one day went to her work, and left her infant in the house in charge of the spirit snake, who was so much annoyed by the screaming of the child that she coiled herself round it and strangled it. The mother came in while the folds of the serpent's body were still wound round her child, and seizing an axe she began to chop the snake to pieces. As she chopped it asunder the parts came together again; but the snake at last could bear it no longer, and cried out weeping, 'I go, and who will help you now?'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. X (1891); not verbatim.

passages.text: She made her way down to the sea, and her track became a water-course. Leaving the island, she swam across first to Ugi, but from thence she could see the Bauro mountain; she went on further to Ulawa, and thence again to the south-east end of Malanta, but even there in clear weather she could see her former home. She crossed therefore to Marau, the south-east part of Guadalcanar nearest to San Cristoval, where the view of the mountain of Bauro is shut off by the nearer hills; there she rests till the present day. Since her departure all things in San Cristoval have deteriorated. Snakes upon the Bauro mountain are venerated as the progeny or representatives of Kahausibware.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. X (1891); not verbatim.

title.en: Manlepei Follows Marawa into the Rock
title.zh: 曼勒佩隨馬拉瓦入石府

region.en: Vanua Lava, Banks Islands, Vanuatu (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 瓦努阿圖班克斯群島瓦努阿瓦島（象徵定位）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded by R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians, 1891, ch. X

source.work: R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians: Studies in their Anthropology and Folk-lore (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1891), ch. X 'Spirits'

summary.en: A few years before Codrington wrote, a man of Vanua Lava followed a small, long-haired vui up a valley; the vui rapped a closing rock, and both passed into a cave that was his house. 'I am Marawa,' he said, and asked for money — and Manlepei prospered ever after, collecting his neighbours' offerings to the spirit.
summary.zh: 瓦努阿瓦島人曼勒佩清晨至河邊，見一長髮小人，尾隨至峽谷盡頭；小人叩石，石開而入，曼勒佩緊隨，石復合。洞中即其家。小人自稱馬拉瓦，許諾若送錢來將再現身。曼勒佩自此興旺，替鄉人轉交供金以求神恩，毫不隱瞞財源。

sensitivity.note: Missionary-anthropologist record (Codrington 1891); living spirit belief recorded within living memory of the 1880s.

passages.text: A man living in Vanua Lava but a few years ago, named Manlepei, going to the river side in early morning, saw a little man with long hanging hair, and followed him up the valley in which the river runs, till they came to a narrow gorge closed by a rock. The vui rapped upon this with his hand and it opened to him; and as Manlepei followed close behind, it shut again upon them both. They were in a cave which was the vui's house.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. X (1891); not verbatim.

passages.text: He said that he was Marawa, and that he would appear again to the man if he would go back to the village and bring him money. Manlepei prospered ever after through Marawa's aid, and he made no secret of the source of his prosperity; he was always ready to receive money from his neighbours on Marawa's behalf, and to procure for them a share in his good will. Marawa, the friend of Qat, was of the lesser folk of spirits who lingered in the islands when Qat and his brothers left them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. X (1891); not verbatim.

title.en: The Nopitu: Spirits That Sing and Pour Out Money

region.en: Mota and Motlav, Banks Islands, Vanuatu (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 瓦努阿圖班克斯群島莫塔島與莫特拉夫島（象徵定位）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded by R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians, 1891, ch. X

source.work: R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians: Studies in their Anthropology and Folk-lore (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1891), ch. X 'Spirits'

summary.en: Certain corporeal spirits called Nopitu possess chosen dancers, who scratch themselves and drop new stringless money, vomit shell-coins, crunch coin instead of yam, and fill a drained coconut with money. At evening fires a tiny, unforgettable voice sings the ordinary Mota songs; some women carry the spirit as an infant, and it is born again as a child.
summary.zh: 莫塔與莫特拉夫島有所謂諾皮圖之靈，附身於人便顯奇蹟：抓撓皮膚即落新錢，震身則錢如雨落於席，啜椰則傾出貝幣琅琅作響，吐於地上；食生紅薯時齒間竟聞錢聲。夜火之旁，一縷細而清甜、一聽難忘之嗓音唱起莫塔之歌，眾人擊鼓相和；靈言『我去矣』，倏然而逝。有女子感到靈入腹，如嬰兒攜於背上，日後竟生為常兒——莫特拉夫島之邦戈洛阿即是。

passages.text: Some vui, spiritual beings yet in some way corporeal, figure strangely in the stories of Mota as Nopitu, and of Motlav as Demhit. The name Nopitu is given both to the spirit and to the person possessed by the spirit, who performs wonders by the power and in the name of the Nopitu who possesses him. Such a one would dance at a festival as no man not possessed by a Nopitu could dance. He would scratch himself, his arm or his head, and new money not yet strung would fall from his fingers; one would shake himself on a mat and unstrung money would pour down into it. He would take a cocoa-nut to drink, and the bystanders would hear money pouring out instead of the liquor, rattling against his teeth.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. X (1891); not verbatim.

passages.text: A party would be sitting round an evening fire, and one of them would hear a voice as if proceeding from his thigh, saying, 'Here am I, give me some food, I am hungry.' He would roast a little red yam, and when it was done fold it in the corner of the mat on which he was sitting; in a little while it would be gone, and then the Nopitu would begin to talk and sing in a voice so small and clear and sweet, that once heard it never could be forgotten; but it sang the ordinary Mota songs, while the men drummed an accompaniment for it. Then it would say, 'I am going'; they would call it, and it was gone. Sometimes a woman would hear a Nopitu say 'Mother, I am coming to you,' and she would feel the spirit entering into her, and it would be born afterwards as an ordinary child. Such a one, named Bongoloa, was not long ago still living at Motlav.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. X (1891); not verbatim.

title.en: Qatgoro the Stone and the Twelve Tangaro Brothers
title.zh: 石母卡特戈羅與十二塔加羅兄弟

region.en: Alo Sepere, Vanua Lava, Banks Islands (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 瓦努阿圖班克斯群島瓦努阿瓦島阿洛塞佩雷村（象徵定位）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded by R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians, 1891, ch. X (Mota text of Deacon Edward Wogale)

source.work: R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians: Studies in their Anthropology and Folk-lore (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1891), ch. X 'Spirits'

summary.en: Qat had a mother, Qatgoro — a stone that burst asunder and brought him forth on the road. He talked at once, named himself, and joined twelve brothers: Tangaro the Wise who understood all things, Tangaro the Fool who knew nothing, and nine more named for the leaves of trees — nettle, bread-fruit, bamboo, cocoa-nut, umbrella-palm.
summary.zh: 卡特非無所自出：其母卡特戈羅本是一石，爆裂而生卡特於途。他生而能言，自問名而自名為卡特。其兄弟十二：長兄塔加羅·基拉基拉拉智者，無所不曉，能教眾人；次兄塔加羅·洛洛龔愚者，一無所知；其餘九人以樹葉為名——蕁麻葉、麵包果葉、竹葉、椰葉、傘棕葉……連卡特共十二人。眾兄弟生而即長，同住阿洛塞佩雷村；其母化為之石，至今猶在。

sensitivity.note: Missionary-era Mota text by a native deacon (Codrington 1891); Sepere clan heritage of Vanua Lava.

passages.text: Qat was not without a beginning, but he had a mother whose name was Qatgoro, and this mother was a stone that burst asunder and brought him forth. He had no father, and he was born on the road. He grew up and talked at once. He asked his mother what his name was, saying that if he had a father or an uncle on his mother's side, one of them would name him; then he gave himself the name of Qat.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. X (1891), Mota text of Edward Wogale; not verbatim.

passages.text: He had brothers also. The first was Tangaro Gilagilala, Tangaro the Wise, who understood all things, and could instruct the rest; the second was Tangaro Loloqong, Tangaro the Fool, who was ignorant of everything, and behaved like a fool; the others were nine more, all Tangaro, twelve in all with Qat. The names of the last nine are made up of the names of the leaves of trees and plants — Nettle-leaf, Bread-fruit-leaf, Bamboo-leaf, Cocoa-nut-leaf, Umbrella-palm-leaf — added to Tangaro, which is no doubt the same with the Tagaro of the New Hebrides and the Tangaroa of the Polynesians. These all grew up as soon as they were born, and they took up their abode in the village Alo Sepere, where their mother, turned into a stone, may yet be seen.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. X (1891), Mota text of Edward Wogale; not verbatim.

title.en: Qat Beats the Pigs Down on All Fours
title.zh: 卡特按豬四足、令直立行

region.en: Vanua Lava, Banks Islands, Vanuatu (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 瓦努阿圖班克斯群島瓦努阿瓦島（象徵定位）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded by R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians, 1891, ch. X (Mota text of Deacon Edward Wogale)

source.work: R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians: Studies in their Anthropology and Folk-lore (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1891), ch. X 'Spirits'

summary.en: Qat made men and pigs at first in the same form; when his brothers remonstrated at the sameness of his creatures, he beat the pigs down to go on all fours and made men walk upright.
summary.zh: 卡特初造人與豬，形貌全同。兄弟們抗議其造物千篇一律，卡特便把豬按伏，使其四足而行，而令直立行走。

passages.text: According to the story told at Mota, Qat made men and pigs at first in the same form, but on his brothers remonstrating with him on the sameness of his creatures, he beat down the pigs to go on all fours and made men walk upright. Man was made of clay, the red clay from the marshy riverside at Vanua Lava. The joke explains why the pig snuffles in the house-yard and the man walks to his garden on his two legs — both creatures of the same maker's hand, separated only by a beating.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. X (1891), Mota text of Edward Wogale; not verbatim.

title.en: Iro Vilgale, the Twig-Ringed First Woman

region.en: Vanua Lava, Banks Islands, Vanuatu (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 瓦努阿圖班克斯群島瓦努阿瓦島（象徵定位）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded by R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians, 1891, ch. X (Mota text of Deacon Edward Wogale)

source.work: R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians: Studies in their Anthropology and Folk-lore (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1891), ch. X 'Spirits'

summary.en: The first woman, Iro Vilgale, was fashioned by Qat of rods and rings of supple twigs, bound and covered with sago-palm spathes exactly as the tall hats of the Qatu ceremonies are made — her name from vil, to bind, and gale, to deceive. When all was finished he saw a smile, and then he knew that she was a living woman.
summary.zh: 首女伊羅維爾加勒乃卡特以柔枝與環所造，如製卡圖儀式高帽之法：紮環於枝、覆以西米棕櫚葉鞘。其名取自 vil（紮）與 gale（騙）。既成，卡特見其微微一笑，便知此為活女子。

sensitivity.note: Missionary-era Mota text (Codrington 1891); cross-ref melanesian-qat-clay-twigs (Dixon version).

passages.text: Man was made of clay, the red clay from the marshy riverside at Vanua Lava. The first woman was Iro Vilgale. Qat took rods and rings of supple twigs and fashioned her as they make the tall hats for the qatu, binding on the rings to the rods, and covering all over with the spathes of sago-palms: hence her name from vil to bind, and gale to deceive. When all was finished he saw a smile, and then he knew that she was a living woman.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. X (1891), Mota text of Edward Wogale; not verbatim.

title.en: Ro Lei in Disguise on the Rock

region.en: Banks Islands, Vanuatu (symbolic pin: Gaua/Mota)
region.zh: 瓦努阿圖班克斯群島（象徵定位：高阿島／莫塔島）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded by R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians, 1891, ch. X

source.work: R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians: Studies in their Anthropology and Folk-lore (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1891), ch. X 'Spirits'

summary.en: Sailing with his brothers, Qat came upon an old woman on a rock offering food to each canoe in turn; every brother drew near, saw her age, and rejected her — but Qat took her into his canoe. She was Ro Lei herself, his much-coveted wife, testing them in disguise.
summary.zh: 卡特與兄弟們揚帆出海，見礁石上立一老嫗，逐舟相邀：『來吃我的食物吧。』兄弟們駛近，見她老邁，皆拒之而去；卡特獨上前提她登舟。原來此老嫗正是眾兄弟覬覦之卡特妻羅萊所扮——她以喬裝驗出誰是真心之人。

passages.text: Iro Lei took her part in these tricks. One day when Qat and his brothers were sailing in their canoes they saw a woman on a point of rock, who called each of them as he came near to come and have some of her food. Each as he drew near and saw that she was an old woman rejected her offer; but Qat came up and took her into his canoe. They had rejected his much-coveted wife, for this was Ro Lei in disguise.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. X (1891); not verbatim.

title.en: Qat Hangs as a Flying-Fox

region.en: Banks Islands, Vanuatu (symbolic pin: Gaua/Mota)
region.zh: 瓦努阿圖班克斯群島（象徵定位：高阿島／莫塔島）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded by R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians, 1891, ch. X

source.work: R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians: Studies in their Anthropology and Folk-lore (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1891), ch. X 'Spirits'

summary.en: On a moonlight night Qat covered himself with boards, flew into a pandanus-tree and hung there like a bat. His brothers shot him and climbed after him one by one; each time he flew off and hung again, until he flew home with all their arrows — which Iro Lei helped hang in the gamal as proof against them.
summary.zh: 月明之夜，卡特誘兄弟們去射狐蝠，自己以木板護身，飛上露兜樹倒掛如蝠。兄弟們輪番射箭攀樹捉拿，他每次掙脫再懸；待眾人箭盡力竭，他攜滿身之箭飛回，取出木板上的箭，與妻子伊羅萊一道把箭掛在男子會所裡。兄弟獵歸，他問收穫如何；眾人自誇射中奇蝠，卡特便請他們看會所中那些箭，認認是誰的。

passages.text: Qat was himself always ready to play tricks on his brothers, but not in malice. One moonlight night he induced them to go and shoot flying foxes, and as they were going covered himself with boards, and flew up into a pandanus-tree and hung there like a bat. His brothers saw him, shot at him, and hit him. He spat out blood upon the ground, and they, making sure that he was wounded, mounted one after another into the tree to take the bat. As each one shot and climbed after him he flew off, and returned to hang again.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. X (1891); not verbatim.

passages.text: When all had shot and climbed up he flew home, took out the arrows which had stuck into his covering of boards, and hung them up in the gamal. When his brothers returned he asked them what sport they had; and when they told how they had shot and hit a wonderful bat, he made them look at the arrows and judge whose they were.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. X (1891); not verbatim.

title.en: The Swollen Nutmeg-Tree and the Floating Bottle
title.zh: 脹大之肉豆蔻樹與漂流之瓶

region.en: Vanua Lava to Maewo, Vanuatu (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 瓦努阿圖：自瓦努阿瓦島至馬埃沃島（象徵定位）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded by R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians, 1891, ch. X

source.work: R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians: Studies in their Anthropology and Folk-lore (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1891), ch. X 'Spirits'

summary.en: Trapped aloft by a brother's 'My nutmeg, swell!' spell while his brothers fled with Ro Lei and the canoe, Qat escaped down Marawa's outstretched hair. Then he shrank into a coconut-shell bottle with his plume, red earth, shell money and last bananas, floated ahead of his brothers' canoe, and revealed himself at Maewo — where he hewed their stolen canoe to pieces with his chopping-song.
summary.zh: 兄弟們趁卡特在樹上張網，由最近者下樹念咒『我的肉豆蔻，脹大！』樹幹脹得抱不攏，卡特困在樹頂，眼睜睜看兄弟們搶走羅萊與獨木舟。他放聲大哭，蜘蛛馬拉瓦聞聲而來，放長髮上樹，卡特攀髮而下。回家後，他收起羽飾、紅土、貝幣與末數枚香蕉，縮身入椰殼瓶中，命母親數三浪，第四小浪時擲瓶入海。瓶漂在兄弟舟前，他們只得跟著漂；他吃蕉擲皮，智者塔加羅識破，眾人不信；有人拾瓶嫌臭而棄。卡特至馬埃沃登岸，坐上灘頭露兜樹頂；兄弟抵岸，他以斧將其舟剁碎，唱道：『剁舟，剁舟，這是誰的舟？馬拉瓦的舟……』剁罷又與兄弟們和好。

passages.text: Again they consulted how they might destroy him, and determined to entrap him while snaring birds. They prepared each one for himself his place in a nutmeg-tree, each in succession further and further from the village, and the tree for Qat much further away than all. Qat mounted into his tree, and as soon as he was busy with his snares his brother nearest to him descended from his own place, ran beneath the tree where Qat was sitting, and said, 'My nutmeg, swell!' The nutmeg-tree instantly grew so large in the trunk that Qat's arms could never clasp it, and all its boughs and branches equally swelled out. His brother ran back, collecting the others as he went into the village; they seized and carried off Ro Lei, dragged down the canoe into the sea, and paddled off at once.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. X (1891); not verbatim.

passages.text: When Qat heard their shell trumpet he knew what had happened, and would have followed them, but the size of the swelled branches made it impossible for him to descend; he tried and tried in vain, and then lifted up his voice and wept. His friend Marawa, the Spider, heard his cries: 'Down with you,' said Marawa, whose hair was exceedingly long and loose; and he sent up his hair to Qat, who descended by it and ran into the village. There he found the rollers of his canoe alone remaining, and sought his wife in vain.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. X (1891); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then Qat went inside his house, and took his cock's-tail plume, his string of the smallest shell-money, his red earth, and his shell hatchet, and asked his mother for his banana fruit. 'They have plucked them all,' she answered, 'except these little ones at the end of the bunch.' Then he took a cocoa-nut-shell bottle and stowed all his things and his food within it, made himself small and took his seat within it, and bade his mother count three waves, and at the fourth small wave to throw it into the sea. So Qat floated on and on in the bottle till he came up to the canoe in which his brothers were, and where he drifted they were forced to follow. He ate a banana and threw the skin into the sea; Tangaro the Wise spoke out: 'It is Qat who has eaten this banana, and has thrown the skin of it here for us, to give us notice that he is not dead.' But the rest of them would not listen to him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. X (1891); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then Qat floated quickly to the shore of Maewo, and emerged from his bottle; he coloured his hair with the red earth, bound his small shell-money round his head, stuck his cock's-tail plume in his hair, took his seat on the top of a male pandanus-tree on the beach, and there he sat and waited for his brothers to come to land. When they came through the reef and up to the shore they looked up and saw him sitting in the pandanus. So they brought their canoe to land, but had no need to haul it up, for Qat made the rocks to rise and bear it high and dry. Qat leaped down upon them with his axe, and hewed the canoe to pieces for them with this song — 'Chop, chop the canoe; whose canoe is it? Marawa's canoe. My brothers tricked me about twisting a string — swell nutmeg-tree — and draw the snare. I had one canoe, my canoe slipped off from me.' So he chopped the canoe to pieces before their face. After this he made friends with them, and bade them live in harmony together.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. X (1891); not verbatim.

title.en: Qat and Qasavara: The Tahitian-Chestnut Fruit
title.zh: 卡特與卡薩瓦拉：伊核果之釁

region.en: Vanua Lava, Banks Islands, Vanuatu (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 瓦努阿圖班克斯群島瓦努阿瓦島（象徵定位）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded by R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians, 1891, ch. X

source.work: R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians: Studies in their Anthropology and Folk-lore (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1891), ch. X 'Spirits'

summary.en: A Tahitian-chestnut fruit floated down the stream from the cannibal ogre Qasavara's tree; the brothers scorned it but Qat took it home. Climbing the tree for more, the foolish brother dropped a fruit on Qasavara's house, and the brothers were killed and boxed. Qat came five days later, dropped a fruit on the house, fought and killed the ogre, found the bones in the food-chest, and blew them alive through a reed — 'if you are my brothers, laugh.'
summary.zh: 兄弟們沐浴時見溪中漂下一枚伊核果，皆棄而不取，獨卡特拾回家中。眾兄弟循溪尋樹攀摘，愚兄一果失手，砸在食人巨人卡薩瓦拉屋頂；巨人怒而出，殺盡兄弟，收入食箱。卡特等了五日，攜弓箭貝斧循溪而至，也投一果砸其屋頂，誘出巨人大戰而誅之；開箱尋兄，只剩白骨。他以蘆管對口吹氣，兄弟骨肉復生——並命他們：『若是我兄弟，便笑。』眾人果然笑起來。

passages.text: Another remarkable series of adventures were Qat's encounters with Qasavara. This was a vui, very strong, a great fighter, tyrant and cannibal, who dwelt in the island which was the home of Qat and his brothers. One day the brothers went to bathe, and found floating down the stream a fruit of the Tahitian chestnut, a make. The others took it up one after another and rejected it, thinking it was not good, but Qat took it and found it good, and gave it to his mother to cook. Each of the brothers as he returned from bathing went to their mother for food; she had nothing but Qat's make, and they each took a bit of it; Tangaro the Fool finished it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. X (1891); not verbatim.

passages.text: Qat sent them to get some more, and following up the stream down which this fruit had floated they came upon the tree. They climbed upon it to gather the chestnuts, and Tangaro the Fool dropped one upon the house of Qasavara, over which the branches hung. Out came the ogre in a rage, seized and killed the brothers, and put them in his food-chest. Qat waited five days, then took his bow and arrows and shell hatchet and went in search. Following the stream he found the tree, and divining what had happened, brought out Qasavara by dropping a make on his house. They fought, and Qat killed Qasavara; then, searching for his brothers, he found their bones in the food-chest. He revived them by blowing through a reed into their mouths, and bidding them, if they were his brothers, laugh.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. X (1891); not verbatim.

title.en: Sleeping in the Rafter, the Post, and the Ridge-Pole

region.en: Vanua Lava, Banks Islands, Vanuatu (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 瓦努阿圖班克斯群島瓦努阿瓦島（象徵定位）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded by R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians, 1891, ch. X

source.work: R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians: Studies in their Anthropology and Folk-lore (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1891), ch. X 'Spirits'

summary.en: Qasavara lodged Qat's party in his gamal to kill them at night; Qat rapped the timbers open and the brothers slept inside rafter, side post, and ridge-pole in turn — while the Fool betrayed every retreat. Each night the ogre smashed an empty timber.
summary.zh: 卡薩瓦拉邀卡特一夥留宿其男子會所，欲夜半殺之。入夜眾人怕極；卡特以指節叩開一椽，兄弟皆入內而眠。夜半巨人持棒弓來殺，遍尋睡處無人，怏怏而返。天明問『你們睡在哪裡？』眾人皆答睡在指定之處，唯愚兄嚷道：『我們就睡在這椽子裡！』兄長大怒。次夜卡特叩開邊柱，眾人睡柱中；巨人又來砸椽，依舊撲空；愚兄又自曝。第三夜睡入正柱，巨人砸邊柱，又是撲空。愚者屢教不改。

passages.text: Qasavara falling in with Qat and his brothers invited them to his village, and made a fire in his oven for them. When it was evening he told them that they were to sleep by themselves in his gamal; but they, knowing that they would be killed, were exceedingly afraid. Night fell and they were very sleepy, and Qat called them to come to bed. He rapped asunder with his knuckles one of the rafters of the gamal, and they all got inside and slept. In the middle of the night Qasavara and his men took clubs and bows and came to kill Qat's party, but not finding them in the sleeping places went back disappointed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. X (1891); not verbatim.

passages.text: At the approach of day the cock crew, and Qat awoke his brothers, bidding them crawl out at once, lest they should be seen leaving the rafter by daylight. So they came out; and when it was clear day Qasavara and his men running to the gamal found Qat and his brothers chatting together. 'Where did you sleep?' asked they. All of them answered that they had slept in the place appointed for them; but Tangaro the Fool cried out, 'We slept in this rafter here,' to the great indignation of his brothers. Qasavara's party again as the night drew on took counsel how they might kill them in the rafter; but that night Qat rapped a side post with his knuckles, it opened and they slept within it. Qasavara's party came in the night and smashed the rafter, found no one there, and again retired. Next morning again they came into the gamal and found Qat and his brothers sitting unconcerned; and again Tangaro the Fool confessed they had been sleeping in the side post.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. X (1891); not verbatim.

passages.text: Next night again Qat opened the great main post and they slept in it, and again Qasavara came and smashed the side post, and found no one there. Tangaro the Fool again made known their retreat, though he had been warned and scolded by his brothers.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. X (1891); not verbatim.

title.en: The Lengthening Casuarina and the Stone of Valour
title.zh: 生長之木麻黃與勇武之石

region.en: Tatgan, Vanua Lava / Gaua, Banks Islands (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 瓦努阿圖班克斯群島塔坦／高阿島（象徵定位）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded by R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians, 1891, ch. X

source.work: R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians: Studies in their Anthropology and Folk-lore (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1891), ch. X 'Spirits'

summary.en: Preparing for a murderous feast, Qat planted a casuarina and drilled his brothers to empty the salt-water vessels and climb the tree. He filled his food-bags leaping round the oven, fled with the ogre chasing, and the lengthening casuarina carried them to the sky, bent down to Tatgan — and flipped Qasavara off, his head knocking the sky; he fell a stone. Sacrifices for valour are offered at that stone, and from his fall come men's baldness and women's breasts.
summary.zh: 卡薩瓦拉謀於宴席殺之。卡特預植木麻黃一棵，密令兄弟：洗手用清水，竹筒水盡即砸筒登樹。宴時眾人依計輪番以取水為名爬樹；卡特獨留灶邊，趁取食之際與巨人隔灶對躍，口呼『這給我兄弟，這給我同伴』，把滿灶食物裝進食物袋。食盡袋滿，他負袋奔向兄弟，巨人追擊連連落空。卡特縱身登樹，喝令『我的木麻黃，長高！』樹身節節拔高，將巨人遠遠拋在下面；樹頂直達天空。卡特又令『彎下來！』樹頂彎至塔坦地面，兄弟逐一落地；最後卡特抓緊樹梢不放——巨人攀至末端。卡特呼『如今我報仇了！』鬆手，樹梢猛彈回去，把卡薩瓦拉拋上天，頭撞天空，墜地成石。今人慾求勇武，皆在那石前獻祭。又傳：自卡薩瓦拉墜天之時，婦女驚惶舉手過頂，男子抱胸在前——故此男人禿頂，婦人乳突。

sensitivity.note: Missionary-era Mota collection (Codrington 1891); valour-sacrifice stone aition.

passages.text: Qasavara now determined to try another course, and to kill them as they were sitting at a feast; that night Qat opened the ridge pole with a rap and they all slept in it. Knowing what was intended, Qat made his preparations to save his brothers by planting a casuarina-tree; and he gave them his instructions what they were to do. 'When they are getting the food ready,' he said, 'wash your hands with the salt-water in the bamboo water-vessels till they are empty; and then when they are looking for salt-water, and wanting some one to go and fill the vessels, two of you are to offer to go; and two are to go at once; and when you get some way off smash the bamboo vessels on the ground, and climb up into the casuarina-tree. All of you are to do this.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. X (1891); not verbatim.

passages.text: They all agreed, and did as they were bid. Then, when the oven was all covered in, Qasavara's men cried out 'Hallo! there is no salt-water! who will fetch some?' 'We two,' said two of Qat's brothers; and they went, and smashed the water-vessels and climbed into the casuarina-tree. So it went on till all his brothers were in the tree, and Qat alone was left beside the oven with Qasavara and his men. Then as they opened the oven Qat sat with a large handful of food-bags beside the oven, and as they were taking out the food Qasavara struck at Qat with his club and missed him. Qat leapt away from him to the other side of the oven, and taking up food from within it cried, 'This for my brother, this for my mate,' and stowed it in the bags. So it went on till all the food in the oven was taken, and all the bags were full.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. X (1891); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then Qat rose and ran to his brothers, and Qasavara after him, hitting at him with his club and missing him as he ran. Then Qat jumped away from him into the tree, and Qasavara climbed after him. Then Qat cried out 'My casuarina, lengthen!' So the casuarina elongated itself between Qat's party and Qasavara, and left him far below. So it went on till the tree top reached the sky. Then said Qat, 'Bend down, my casuarina!' and the tree bent its top down to Tatgan, and they all one after another got down to the ground there, and Qat the last of them. As he reached the ground he held fast on to the top of the casuarina and waited before letting it go; and Qasavara followed down after them and reached the end. Then cried Qat, 'Now I revenge myself.' 'Ah, Qat!' cried Qasavara, 'do me no harm; take me kindly for one of your household, and I will work for you.' 'No, indeed,' said Qat, 'but I will revenge myself for the mischief you have done me.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. X (1891); not verbatim.

passages.text: So he let go the tip of the casuarina-tree, and the tree sprang back and flipped off Qasavara, and his head knocked against the sky, and he fell back upon the earth; and there he lay at length upon his face, and turned into a stone. And now they offer sacrifices at that stone for valour; if any one desires to be valiant and strong in fighting, he offers at that stone, which they say is Qasavara.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. X (1891); not verbatim.

title.en: Qat's Canoe and the Deluge of Gaua
title.zh: 卡特之舟與高阿島洪水

region.en: Lake Tas, Gaua, Banks Islands (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 瓦努阿圖班克斯群島高阿島塔斯湖（象徵定位）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded by R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians, 1891, ch. X

source.work: R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians: Studies in their Anthropology and Folk-lore (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1891), ch. X 'Spirits'

summary.en: On the great forest plain where now lies the lake of Gaua, Qat built a giant canoe, loaded into it his wife, brothers, and every living creature down to the ants, and covered it. Then came a deluge of rain; the hollow island filled, the waters burst the hills at the great waterfall, and the canoe tore its own channel to the sea and vanished — taking the best of everything with Qat, whose return the people still awaited when the first missionaries landed.
summary.zh: 高阿島中部今塔斯湖所在，昔日乃大林原。卡特伐巨木造大舟，兄弟譏笑：『這麼大的舟，怎麼弄得下海？』他只答：『你們等著瞧。』舟成，他載上妻子與兄弟，又收盡島上生靈，連螞蟻也不落下，然後與他們一同閉身艙內，蓋上舟蓋。大雨滂沱而至，全島窪地積水成湖，水衝破周圍山丘——今之大瀑布即彼決口——巨舟自衝水道出海而去。島民相信，世上最好的東西都隨卡特走了；他們盼望他回來。宣教師帕特森初登莫塔島時，有人喊：『卡特帶著兄弟們回來了！』多年後一艘商船在高阿島礁上失事，老人們望著它駛向瀑布水道，喊道：『卡特回來了，他的舟認得回家的路！』

sensitivity.note: Missionary-era Mota collection (Codrington 1891). Codrington explicitly notes the flood story predates Noah-teaching. Flood cluster cross-ref.

passages.text: It was from Gaua that the story makes Qat to have taken his departure from the world. Where now in the centre of that island is the great lake, the Tas, there was formerly a great plain covered with forest. Qat cut himself a large canoe there out of one of the largest trees. While making it he was often ridiculed by his brothers, and asked how he would ever get so large a canoe to the sea. He answered always that they would see by-and-by.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. X (1891); not verbatim.

passages.text: When the canoe was finished he took inside it his wife and brothers, collected the living creatures of the island, even those so small as ants, and shut himself with them inside the canoe, to which he had made a covering. Then came a deluge of rain; the great hollow of the island became full of water, which burst through the surrounding hills where now descends the great waterfall of Gaua. The canoe tore a channel for itself out into the sea and disappeared. The people believed that the best of everything was taken from the islands when Qat so left them, and they looked forward to his return.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. X (1891); not verbatim.

passages.text: When for the first time Bishop Patteson and his companions went ashore at Mota, some of the natives now living remember that it was said that Qat and his brothers were returned. Some years after that a small trading vessel ran on the reef at Gaua, and was lost. The old people, seeing her apparently standing in to the channel of the waterfall stream, cried out that Qat was come again, and that his canoe knew her own way home. It is likely now that the story will be told of eight persons in the canoe; but it is certain that the story is older than any knowledge of Noah's ark among the people.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. X (1891); not verbatim.

title.en: Natei and the Visitors from the Inland Village

region.en: Nelua, Santa Cruz, Solomon Islands (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 所羅門群島聖克魯斯內盧阿村（象徵定位）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded by R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians, 1891, ch. X

source.work: R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians: Studies in their Anthropology and Folk-lore (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1891), ch. X 'Spirits'

summary.en: Young Natei, hunting feather-money birds far inland, met a stranger who led him up a hidden path to gardens and a village whose people promised to visit Nelua in five days. The visitors entered Natei's house and were never seen again — but the house hung with feather-money; they were vui, and from that day Natei thrived.
summary.zh: 聖克魯斯青年納泰入深山尋製羽幣之鳥，遇一 stranger 引他沿隱徑上溯，至有良園與村莊之地。村人問明他住在內盧阿，約定五日後往訪。五日後，內盧阿村人見一群自內陸而來的人打聽納泰；他們進了納泰的屋子，便再無人見過。納泰歸家，見屋中掛滿羽幣——來者非人，乃 vui 之屬，皆蓄長直之髮。自此人們送錢送物託納泰向他的朋友討恩惠，納泰從此發跡。

passages.text: When he was a young man, they say, he was following the upward course of a narrow valley looking for birds to make feather-money, and advanced far inland into the forest. A person met him and asked him who he was, and he answered that he was a man. To Natei's like enquiry the same answer was made. This person then took him by a very good path up the valley, which narrowed into a ravine. This opened again into a space in which were good gardens and a village. The people there enquired of Natei where he lived, and promised him that they would visit him at Nelua in five days; then he returned.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. X (1891); not verbatim.

passages.text: Five days after the people of Nelua saw some people coming to their village, whom they took to be men from some inland place, and enquiring for Natei. His house was shewn to them and they entered it, and were never seen again. When he arrived and went into his house he found it hung round with feather-money brought to him by his visitors. It was known then that these were not mere men, and it was remembered that they had long, straight hair. After this people would give Natei money and other things to obtain the favour of his friends, with whom he still kept up communication, and from that time he has thriven and risen in the world.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. X (1891); not verbatim.

title.en: Tagaro of Maewo Turns the Island Upside Down
title.zh: 馬埃沃之塔加羅掀島東去

region.en: Maewo (Aurora Island), Vanuatu (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 瓦努阿圖馬埃沃島（奧羅拉島）（象徵定位）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded by R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians, 1891, ch. X

source.work: R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians: Studies in their Anthropology and Folk-lore (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1891), ch. X 'Spirits'

summary.en: Tagaro lived at Hombio on Maewo in endless wonder: his coconuts increased as he ate them, scooped dry nuts filled again. Angry that someone stole his pig, he turned the island upside down and went off eastward in his canoe taking the best of everything, never to return; he put out the fire, but threw back a fire-stick; his shell trumpet lies on the beach as a rock, and Lepers' Island is his canoe.
summary.zh: 塔加羅居馬埃沃島洪比奧之地，事事神奇：椰子越吃越多，掏空的乾椰又自動填滿。後因有人偷他的豬，他大怒，把整座島翻了個底朝天，攜走世上一切最好的東西，乘舟自東海岸向東而去，永不復返。他熄滅了火，卻回頭擲回一根火把；他的貝螺號躺在灘上化為岩石；麻瘋島便是他的獨木舟。洪比奧之地至今至聖，他的薯蔓仍攀滿那座名為『薯之會所』的屋。

passages.text: Tagaro was a vui. Yet the stories of Tagaro deal with him as the stories of the Banks' Islands deal with Qat. His companion was Suqe-matua, who in all things was contrary to him. Tagaro lived at Mambarambara, and particularly at Hombio, not far from Tanoriki. He was not born there, but there he lived, made his canoe, built his house and his gamal, and created and raised his food. His life was full of wonders; his cocoa-nuts increased as he ate them; dry nuts out of which he scooped the meat filled up again.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. X (1891); not verbatim.

passages.text: Finally Tagaro became angry because some one stole his pig, and went off to Mamalu, no one knows where; he turned the island upside down, and went off eastwards in his canoe from the east coast of the island, taking with him the best of everything, and never to return. He put out the fire, but threw back a fire-stick; his shell trumpet lies on the beach in the form of a rock; Lepers' Island is his canoe. His place at Hombio is very sacred; his yams still remain there, and trail over a gamal called the gamal dam, the yam gamal.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. X (1891); not verbatim.

title.en: Tagaro and the Forked Head of Suqe

region.en: Araga (Pentecost Island), Vanuatu (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 瓦努阿圖彭特科斯特島（阿臘加）（象徵定位）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded by R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians, 1891, ch. X

source.work: R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians: Studies in their Anthropology and Folk-lore (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1891), ch. X 'Spirits'

summary.en: In Araga, Tagaro came down from heaven with ten brothers; Suqe belonged to the earth, his head forked, with two thoughts in it. Whatever Tagaro did was right, Suqe always wrong: men should die only five days, six nights to one day, plant the scooped yam-meat not the rind. Tagaro banished him to a bottomless chasm inland, where he rules the ghosts of the dead; Tagaro made the plain country by treading it with his feet.
summary.zh: 阿臘加（彭特科斯特島）傳說：塔加羅自天而降，另有十位兄弟；蘇蓋則屬地，頭分兩叉，一頭兩念。塔加羅所為皆對，蘇蓋所言皆錯：他主張人死五日即活、一夜頂六晝、種薯要種掏空的薯肉而非薯皮。塔加羅最後把他趕去內陸一處無底深淵，命他在那裡管轄死者之魂。塔加羅以足踏地，踏平處成平原，未踏處便是山丘。

passages.text: In Araga, Whitsuntide Island, immediately south of Maewo, Tagaro has ten brothers, besides Suqe, who accompanies and thwarts him. Tagaro came down from heaven, made men and other things, and went back again to heaven. Suqe belonged to the earth; his head was forked, therefore he had two thoughts in it. Whatever Tagaro did or made was right, Suqe was always wrong; he would have men die only for five days; he wanted to have six nights to one day; he planted the scooped meat of the yam, not the rind.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. X (1891); not verbatim.

passages.text: Tagaro sent him to a place where is a bottomless chasm, somewhere inland in Araga, where he rules over the ghosts of the dead. Tagaro when on earth, though a vui, had a human form, with superhuman power. He made the plain country by treading the ground with his feet; where he did not tread are the hills.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. X (1891); not verbatim.

title.en: The Boy Who Shot an Arrow into the Sky

region.en: Araga (Pentecost Island), Vanuatu (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 瓦努阿圖彭特科斯特島（阿臘加）（象徵定位）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded by R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians, 1891, ch. X

source.work: R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians: Studies in their Anthropology and Folk-lore (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1891), ch. X 'Spirits'

summary.en: Tagaro fathered a boy on earth who kept asking who his father was. Told he was in heaven, the boy shot up an arrow of flowering-reed that stuck in the sky and became a banyan-root; mother and son climbed to heaven and found Tagaro fashioning images of himself from salite-fruit. Tagaro consented to return — but cut the root above them as he descended, going back to heaven while they came down to Atambulu, the original seat of men.
summary.zh: 塔加羅在人間生有一子，孩兒追問父親是誰，母答在天堂。孩子定要上天見父，母親便為他製蘆葦弓箭。他一箭射上天去，箭中天而化為榕樹氣根，母子攀根而上。天上見塔加羅坐在莎麗特樹上，正用果子捏塑自己的模樣；他擲一枚給孩子，母親認出相貌，告知那就是父親。塔加羅允諾同返人間；然下降時，他在自己下方、母子之上把根割斷，自己回天，母子落到阿坦布盧——那島上人類最初的居地。

passages.text: He had no wife or children of his own kind, but he became the father of a boy on earth. The boy kept asking his mother who his father was, and was told that he was in heaven. Then he must needs go to heaven to see his father, and his mother made him a bow and an arrow of an ere, a flowering reed. He shot up and hit the sky; his ere turned into something like the aerial root of a banyan, up which the two climbed to heaven. There they found Tagaro sitting in a salite-tree, and fashioning images of himself out of the fruit. One of these he threw to the boy, who took it to his mother. She recognised the features, and told the boy it was his father.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. X (1891); not verbatim.

passages.text: Tagaro consented to go back with them; but as he descended he cut the line above them and below himself, and went back to heaven, while they came down to Atambulu, the original seat of men in that island — the boy and his mother left standing on the shore of Atambulu with the man of their house gone back up the broken ladder to the sky.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. X (1891); not verbatim.

title.en: The Two Spirit Women on the Beach

region.en: Lepers Island (Aoba), Vanuatu (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 瓦努阿圖麻瘋島（安巴埃）（象徵定位）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded by R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians, 1891, ch. X

source.work: R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians: Studies in their Anthropology and Folk-lore (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1891), ch. X 'Spirits'

summary.en: Following stolen coconuts, a man found two female vui on the beach, one beautiful, one covered with sores, both hungry. Asked to choose, he took them both — and each gave him a stone full of mana, one for ten barrow-pigs, one for ten sows, promising to help him rise in the Suqe. To this day his wives find fish caught and lying ready on the beach.
summary.zh: 有人發現椰子被偷，循足跡至灘頭，遇兩個女性 vui，自言飢餓。他許諾供食，搬來四大籃。一女貌美，一女滿身瘡;她們問他要哪一個，他答『兩個都要』。二女各贈一枚滿蓄瑪那之石：一枚可得十頭閹豬，一枚可得十頭母豬，並許諾永遠幫他得豬，使他在蘇蓋等級中步步高升。這些女子乃掌豬之靈；至今他的妻子們下灘捕魚，總見魚已捕好躺著等她們。

passages.text: There is a man still living who one day followed his two wives down to the beach, and noticed there that some cocoa-nuts had been stolen from a tree he had made. Following footsteps he found two female vui, who said they were hungry. He promised them food and brought it to them — four baskets-full. One of the women was beautiful, the other full of sores. They asked him which he would have, and he answered that he would take them both.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. X (1891); not verbatim.

passages.text: Thereupon each gave him a stone full of mana, one to get him ten barrow-pigs, the other for ten sows; and they promised always to help him to get pigs, that he might mount to greatness in the Suqe. These women were vui, whose power lay in pigs; nevertheless, to this day, when the man's wives go down to the beach for their fishing, they find fish caught and lying ready for them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. X (1891); not verbatim.

title.en: Tagaro Brings Night in a Shell

region.en: Lepers Island (Aoba), Vanuatu (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 瓦努阿圖麻瘋島（安巴埃）（象徵定位）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded by R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians, 1891, ch. X

source.work: R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians: Studies in their Anthropology and Folk-lore (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1891), ch. X 'Spirits'

summary.en: It was Tagaro who went to Maewo and brought back night in a shell. When he let it out and darkness crept over the sky, men wept and beat their houses.
summary.zh: 正是塔加羅往馬埃沃去，用一枚貝殼把夜帶了回來。他放出夜來，黑暗爬滿天空，人們號哭起來，捶打自家的屋子。

sensitivity.note: Missionary-era record (Codrington 1891); cross-ref qat-creation and melanesian-banks-night-released (Qat version).

passages.text: It was Tagaro also who went to Maewo and brought back night in a shell. When he let it out and darkness crept over the sky, men wept and beat their houses — the first nightfall of the Lepers' Islands, received with wailing rather than welcome.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. X (1891); not verbatim.

title.en: Tagaro's Little Son and the Garden of Crowns

region.en: Lepers Island (Aoba), Vanuatu (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 瓦努阿圖麻瘋島（安巴埃）（象徵定位）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded by R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians, 1891, ch. X

source.work: R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians: Studies in their Anthropology and Folk-lore (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1891), ch. X 'Spirits'

summary.en: Tagaro was father of ten sons, the last, Tagaro-mbiti, exceedingly small. His nine brothers planted leaves and vines and called him idle, not knowing he was wise: he had planted the crown of the caladium, the suckers of the banana, the rind of the yam — and when the season came his garden was full of food.
summary.zh: 塔加羅有十子，最幼者塔加羅姆比提，身量極小。九位兄長出門耕作，只種芋葉、蕉芽、薯藤，見幼弟留家腿上生瘡，便罵他懶惰，不知他實則最能。幼弟所種者乃芋之頂冠、蕉之吸芽、薯之皮層——季節一到，兄長們無食可吃，幼弟的園中卻滿是收成。

passages.text: Tagaro is represented also as the father of ten sons, of whom Tagaro-mbiti, the Little, was the last, and exceedingly small. His brothers went out to work, but he stayed at home with a sore on his leg. They planted the leaves of the edible caladium, the top shoot of the banana, the vine of the yam; but when they were gone he took the crown of the caladium, the suckers of the banana, the rind of the yam, and planted them. His brothers scolded him for idleness, not knowing what he was about; but when the season came round and they had nothing to eat, he shewed them his garden full of food.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. X (1891); not verbatim.

title.en: The Tavogivogi Changelings

region.en: Lepers Island (Aoba), Vanuatu (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 瓦努阿圖麻瘋島（安巴埃）（象徵定位）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded by R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians, 1891, ch. X

source.work: R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians: Studies in their Anthropology and Folk-lore (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1891), ch. X 'Spirits'

summary.en: Beings called Tavogivogi — 'changelings' — appear as a youth or woman to entice one of the opposite sex; the one who yields dies. Their only test is to ask the name of a tree, for a wrong answer shows deceit; successful or not, the Tavogivogi vanishes suddenly, like a bird, and the seduced youth sickens at home and never recovers.
summary.zh: 有所謂塔沃基沃基之靈，意即『易形者』：或化青年、或化女子，專誘異性；一旦失身相從，其人必死。其唯一驗法是問附近樹木之名——答錯即見其騙。無論得手與否，塔沃基沃基會突然消失，『如鳥一般』化為鳥獸而去。受誘的青年回家便一病不起，自知遭了靈算，終無可救。

passages.text: Beings called Tavogivogi must be classed as spirits: they are certainly not human beings. A Tavogivogi is not thought ever to have the appearance of a snake; one of them appears in the form of a youth or woman, in order to entice one of the opposite sex, and the young man or woman who yields to the seduction dies. There is no outward sign of the real character of the Tavogivogi, but the test is to ask the name of a tree, and a wrong answer will shew that there is deceit.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. X (1891); not verbatim.

passages.text: Successful or not the Tavogivogi suddenly disappears, 'like a bird,' but in the form of a bird or other creature. The young man goes home and sickens; he remembers the sudden disappearance, knows what has befallen him, and never recovers. The name means 'changeling,' from the word, in the Banks' Islands, wog, to change the form.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. X (1891); not verbatim.
